c.tagline: Lakeside towers and the world in one city

emergency.note: 911 covers all emergencies; 311 handles city services and 211 social services.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Kensington Market: the bohemian open-air market's vintage shops and global food stalls
hood_landmark.The Annex: the Bata Shoe Museum amid leafy streets of Victorian mansions
hood_landmark.Yorkville: Mink Mile luxury shopping near the Royal Ontario Museum
hood_landmark.Distillery District: the cobblestoned Victorian Gooderham & Worts distillery complex
hood_landmark.Queen West: Graffiti Alley's block-long murals and indie boutiques

avoid.reason: No true no-go zones, though the Moss Park area around Sherbourne and Dundas East feels rough after dark.
Keep usual awareness late at night around Yonge-Dundas and on late-night transit, and never leave valuables in parked cars.

hood_desc: Kensington Market is a bohemian, multicultural warren of vintage shops, street food, cafes and murals, ideal for young, budget and eclectic travelers seeking an offbeat vibe.
The Annex is a leafy, intellectual neighborhood near the University of Toronto with Victorian homes, bookish cafes and Bloor Street eats, suited to students and relaxed stays.
Yorkville is Toronto's luxury district of designer boutiques, upscale galleries, fine dining and five-star hotels, perfect for high-end shoppers and affluent visitors.
The Distillery District is a pedestrian-only Victorian industrial precinct of cobblestones, art galleries, boutiques and restaurants, great for couples and a charming historic setting.
Queen West is a hip, trendy strip of independent fashion, art galleries, music venues and nightlife, appealing to creatives and younger travelers wanting a cool scene.

water.note: Tap water is safe and among the most rigorously tested in the world.

transit.pay: Easiest: tap a contactless credit/debit card or phone at any reader - one adult fare (about C$3.30 / US$2.40) covers 2 hours of transfers across subway, streetcars and buses. Or get a PRESTO card (C$6) from station fare machines or Shoppers Drug Mart pharmacies. The same tap works on the UP Express airport train and GO trains.
transit.hours: Subway runs about 6am-1:30am (from 8am Sundays); Blue Night buses and streetcars cover major routes overnight.

transit.m: UP Express to Union Station (25 min)
TTC 900 bus to Kipling station then subway downtown (55 min)

food.name: Peameal bacon sandwich
food.desc: Toronto's signature sandwich: thick slices of cornmeal-crusted back bacon griddled and piled on a kaiser roll with mustard.

places.name: Carousel Bakery
places.note: The stall that made the sandwich famous; expect a line at the counter.

places.name: Paddington's Pump
places.note: Upstairs diner doing a plated version with eggs if you want to sit down.

places.name: When the Pig Came Home
places.note: Deli with a cult following for its smoky, generously stacked peameal sandwich.

food.name: Jamaican patty
food.desc: A flaky turmeric-yellow pastry filled with spiced beef, chicken or vegetables - often eaten inside a coco bread for the full Toronto move.

places.name: Randy's Patties
places.note: Eglinton West institution since 1979; beef patties straight from the oven.

places.name: Patty King International
places.note: Bakery counter with a long list of fillings and proper coco bread.

places.name: Golden Patty
places.note: Cheap, fast and central; good stop while wandering the market.

food.name: Butter tart
food.desc: A Canadian pastry shell filled with butter, sugar and egg that bakes into a gooey caramel centre. Runny or firm, raisins or not, is a real debate.

places.name: Wanda's Pie in the Sky
places.note: Bakery-cafe turning out award-winning tarts and whole pies daily.

places.name: The Rolling Pin
places.note: Small-batch bakery with a cult following for its buttery tarts.

places.name: St Lawrence Market
places.note: Several bakery stalls sell them; easy to taste-test a few in one visit.

food.name: Chinatown classics and dim sum
food.desc: Toronto's Chinatowns run from Spadina to Scarborough, serving Cantonese roast meats, hand-folded dumplings and cart-service dim sum.

places.name: Rol San
places.note: Late-night Spadina standby for dim sum ordered off a checklist.

places.name: Mother's Dumplings
places.note: Northern-style dumplings and noodles made by hand in the front window.

places.name: Asian Legend
places.note: Reliable soup dumplings and scallion pancakes in a comfortable room.

food.name: Trinidadian roti
food.desc: A soft dhalpuri wrap folded around curried goat, chicken or channa - a Caribbean staple that became a Toronto lunchtime default.

places.name: Gandhi Roti
places.note: Long queues for enormous Indian-Caribbean rotis, made to order.

places.name: Ali's Roti Shop
places.note: West-end institution for goat and boneless chicken roti.

places.name: Bacchus Roti
places.note: Family-run spot with vegetarian options and a hot house pepper sauce.

food.name: Veal sandwich
food.desc: Toronto's Italian contribution: breaded veal cutlet on a crusty bun with tomato sauce, provolone and grilled peppers, eaten leaning forward.

places.name: California Sandwiches
places.note: The original 1967 location; the sandwich other shops are measured against.

places.name: San Francesco Foods
places.note: Clinton Street counter serving the same messy classic since 1959.

food.name: Caesar cocktail
food.desc: Canada's own brunch drink: vodka, Clamato, hot sauce and Worcestershire on a celery-salt rim, garnished with anything from a pickle to a slider.

places.name: The Drake Hotel
places.note: Brunch institution with a well-made Caesar and a busy patio.

places.name: Sneaky Dee's
places.note: Dive-bar landmark; nachos and Caesars in the same order.

places.name: Bar Hop
places.note: Beer bar that also does a properly dressed Caesar.

food.name: Ontario craft beer
food.desc: Toronto has dozens of breweries pouring within city limits, from hop-forward IPAs to crisp lagers made in old industrial buildings.

places.name: Bellwoods Brewery
places.note: The city's cult brewery; hazy IPAs and sours plus a leafy patio.

places.name: Steam Whistle Brewing
places.note: Pilsner brewed in the historic John Street Roundhouse by the CN Tower.

places.name: Left Field Brewery
places.note: Baseball-themed east-end taproom with a rotating tap list.

landmarks: CN Tower
This iconic 553-meter communications tower dominates the Toronto skyline and offers a glass floor and observation decks with sweeping city and lake views.
Casa Loma
A fairy-tale Edwardian castle complete with towers, secret passages, and manicured gardens, offering one of the city's most whimsical photo backdrops.
Royal Ontario Museum (ROM)
Canada's largest museum is instantly recognizable for the angular crystalline Michael Lee-Chin Crystal addition jutting from its historic facade.
Toronto Sign at Nathan Phillips Square
The giant 3D 'TORONTO' letters in front of City Hall are one of the most popular photo spots in the city, especially when illuminated at night.
Distillery District
A pedestrian-only Victorian industrial village of restored brick warehouses filled with galleries, cafes, and cobblestone lanes, beloved for its historic charm.
Toronto City Hall
This striking modernist building with two curved towers cradling a domed council chamber is a bold architectural landmark facing Nathan Phillips Square.
St. Lawrence Market
Named one of the world's best food markets, this historic market hall is packed with vendors selling fresh produce, meats, and Toronto's famous peameal bacon sandwiches.
Toronto Islands
A chain of car-free islands in Lake Ontario offering beaches, bike trails, and arguably the best skyline views of downtown Toronto across the water.
Ripley's Aquarium of Canada
Located at the base of the CN Tower, this aquarium's moving underwater tunnel through a shark-filled tank is a top family and photo attraction.
Kensington Market
A colorful, bohemian multicultural neighborhood of vintage shops, street murals, and food stalls that offers some of Toronto's most vibrant street photography.

intl.to: New York City (United States) via Niagara Falls & Albany

train.note: The once-daily Maple Leaf leaves Toronto Union Station early in the morning; US border checks happen at the Niagara Falls crossing, so carry your passport. VIA Rail trains to Montreal, Ottawa and the rest of Canada also depart from Union Station.

bus.note: Cross-border coaches leave from the Union Station Bus Terminal downtown; you clear US immigration at the border, so have your passport ready.

ferry.note: No international ferries from Toronto. The City of Toronto runs short local ferries to the Toronto Islands from the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal at the foot of Bay Street (tickets via toronto.ca).

half.name: Niagara Falls
half.blurb: The thundering cascades are a natural wonder, with boat rides right to the misty base.

half.name: Niagara-on-the-Lake
half.blurb: A charming heritage town amid wineries, known for icewine, blossoms and Victorian streets.

half.name: Elora
half.blurb: A picturesque village beside a dramatic limestone gorge and river ideal for summer tubing.

full.name: Muskoka
full.blurb: Cottage country of glittering lakes, granite shores and pine forests, gorgeous in autumn.

full.name: Algonquin Provincial Park
full.blurb: A vast wilderness of lakes and forest, prime for canoeing, hiking and moose spotting.

full.name: Bruce Peninsula
full.blurb: Turquoise waters, rugged cliffs and the famous Grotto sea cave along Georgian Bay.
